excerpt: GLB Export is Here — Proper Materials, Two UV Channels, One File Level Modeller can now export your levels as GLB (glTF 2.0 binary) — alongside the existing OBJ export. This is a big quality-of-life upgrade if you're bringing levels into…
body:
GLB Export is Here — Proper Materials, Two UV Channels, One File

Level Modeller can now export your levels as GLB (glTF 2.0 binary) — alongside the existing OBJ export. This is a big quality-of-life upgrade if you're bringing levels into Unity, Godot, Unreal, Blender, or three.js.

Why GLB?

OBJ only supports a single UV channel, so getting a lightmap-ready mesh out meant baking everything into one texture atlas. GLB doesn't have that limitation — it carries multiple UV channels and real material definitions natively, so your level exports the way it's actually built:

  • TEXCOORD_0 — the tiled box-projection UVs, with one material per texture, exactly as you see it in the editor.
  • TEXCOORD_1 — a clean, non-overlapping lightmap unwrap, ready for the lightmap baker in your engine. And here's the nice part: you don't need to bake lighting first — if the unwrap doesn't exist yet, the exporter generates it automatically on export.

Export options at a glance

  • Mesh scale — uniform multiplier, so you can match your engine's units.
  • Pivot point — choose what lands at the origin: scene origin, center of bounds, bottom center (the model "stands" on the origin), the selected object, or custom coordinates.
  • Texture storage — your choice:
    • Embedded (default): everything packed into a single, self-contained .glb — one file to drag and drop.
    • External: images referenced as separate files, copied either next to the .glb or into a textures/ subfolder.
  • Baked lightmap — if you've baked lighting in Level Modeller, you can include the lightmap in the file as the material's occlusion texture, sampled from UV1.
  • Atlas mode — the OBJ-style workflow is still here for pipelines that want exactly one material: all albedo baked into a single texture laid out by the lightmap UVs, with an optional "burn baked lighting into the atlas" toggle that multiplies your baked lighting straight into the albedo. Great for quick previews and engines/renderers where you want zero material setup.
  • Vertex tints — per-object color tints export as vertex colors (COLOR_0), so tinted geometry looks the same outside the editor.

Textures are embedded as-is when they're PNG/JPEG; other formats (TGA, BMP, …) are converted to PNG automatically, so the file always loads everywhere.

The OBJ (+MTL) export isn't going anywhere — but if your target understands glTF, GLB is now the recommended path.

As always, let me know if an exported file misbehaves in your engine of choice!

title: OBJ Export: Material & Texture Fixes
excerpt: OBJ Export — Three Fixes 1. map_Kd lines in the MTL (user-reported bug) The MTL file only contained newmtl , Kd , Ka , Ks , Ns , d — no map_Kd line, so renderers that rely on it (Raylib, others) showed no texture. Fix: ExportObjOptions now…
body:
OBJ Export — Three Fixes

1. map_Kd lines in the MTL (user-reported bug)
The MTL file only contained newmtl, Kd, Ka, Ks, Ns, d — no map_Kd line, so renderers that rely on it (Raylib, others) showed no texture. Fix: ExportObjOptions now carries a texture_paths map (texture name → absolute file path) and an optional copy_textures flag. In OnExportOBJ, the map is populated from g_projectSettings.textures before calling the exporter. ObjWriter stores a mat_to_tex map built at triangle-add time. write_mtl now emits map_Kd <path> for every material that has a resolved path. When copy_textures is true, the files are copied into a textures/ subfolder next to the OBJ and the MTL references them with a relative path.

2. Duplicate materials
Every texture previously produced three MTL entries: FLOOR_X, CEIL_X, WALL_X. A map with ten unique textures generated thirty material slots in Blender. The fix removes the prefix entirely — the material name is now the texture name itself. Floor, ceiling, and wall surfaces that share the same texture automatically share one MTL entry.

New: OBJ Export Options

Exporting your level to OBJ just got a lot more flexible. Instead of dumping the mesh at a fixed size and position, File → Export to OBJ… now opens an options dialog first.

  • Center of first sector — handy when your starting room is the natural anchor
  • Center of whole map — keeps everything balanced around (0,0,0)
  • Player start position — origin lands right where the player spawns
  • Custom coordinates — type exact X/Y if you know precisely what you want
  • Origin (0,0) — the original behavior, no recentering

The dialog also shows a live readout of which map point will end up at the origin, and it automatically disables options your current map can't satisfy (e.g. "Player start" when no player is placed).

Small quality-of-life change, but it removes a whole round-trip of fixing scale and pivot after every export. Enjoy!

body:
Blender-style transform hotkeys (G / R / S)

This is the bigger one: we added modal transforms, just like you're used to in Blender. No more dragging gizmo arrows — one key press and a mouse move, and you're transforming instantly.

The basics:

  • G – grab (move)
  • R – rotate
  • S – scale

Press the key, move the mouse, and the selection follows. Left click or Enter confirms, right click or Esc cancels (everything snaps back to its original state).

Axis constraints: while transforming, press X, Y or Z to lock the operation to a single axis. Press the same key again to release it. The constrained axis is shown with a colored guide line (X = red, Y = green, Z = blue).

Exact numeric input: just type a value mid-transform. For example G Z 2 moves exactly 2 units along Z; R X 45 rotates 45 degrees around X. - and . are supported, and Backspace edits your input.

Visual feedback: a header at the top-center of the viewport shows the current mode and value (e.g. Rotate Z: 45), so you always know where you stand.

All of this works in both Object and Edit mode (on objects, or on selected vertices/edges/faces) and is fully integrated with the undo/redo system.

⚠️ Change: the R key previously switched to the scale gizmo — it now triggers rotation, matching Blender. The Q (select), W (move) and E (rotate) gizmo shortcuts are still available.

Yellow pivot dot while modeling

A small yellow dot now marks the pivot point of the selected model — the reference point that rotation and scaling happen around.

  • In Object mode the dot sits on the object's origin (or the shared center when multiple objects are selected), and it's visible in every tool mode — even "Select" mode, where no gizmo is otherwise drawn.
  • In Edit mode (vertex/edge/face editing) the dot stays on the model's origin, so you always have a reference point while working on the geometry.

The marker is drawn in world space, exactly on the pivot, and uses the same yellow tone as the selection outline for a consistent look.

We have reached the first milestone. Version 1.0 is already a highly useful tool for animators and game developers alike.

What is an even bigger step forward:

FBX export — brand-new system (the biggest item)

  • New standalone MeshLoaderFBX_Export.cpp (~1,370 lines) and a Blender-style export popup with a full settings set (FbxExportSettings + presets).

  • Materials: diffuse + normal map + emissive map, PBR scalars (metallic/roughness), and per-face multi-material (submesh) support.
  • Texture path modes: Absolute / Relative / Strip Path / Copy (copies textures next to the FBX).
  • Vertex color round-trip (import → edit → export).

FBX import — major rework

  • Rewritten MeshLoaderFBX.cpp, new FbxNode.h, FBX animation import, multi-material import, texture path resolution, import settings + presets UI.

OBJ import/export UI — dedicated settings & preset system (ObjImport/ExportSettings, …Presets).

Material & UV system

  • Multi-UV (multiple UV channels), large UV editor panel rewrite, 2D drawing gizmo (Gizmo2D).

title: Level Editor 1.2

body:
Level mirroring fix (Level Editor → Unity / OBJ)

The 2D editor works in Y-down screen space, which was causing exported levels to come out mirrored along their north-south axis. We fixed the handedness properly for each target: Unity (left-handed) now maps mapY → -Z, with triangle winding swapped to keep culling correct, thing positions negated on Z, and thing rotation corrected to 90 + angle. Importantly, we then realized the OBJ exporter is right-handed and needs no negation at all — the two targets are mirror opposites — so the OBJ path was reverted to write Z verbatim. Net result: geometry now lands the right way round in both Unity and Blender. Also cleaned a stray buildlog.txt out of the repo.

Recent textures on the toolbar (Level Editor)

Added a quick-apply row of 5 recent-texture slots to the toolbar. Picking a texture from a sidebar combo (floor / ceiling / wall) pushes it onto a de-duplicated most-recently-used list; clicking a toolbar slot then applies that texture straight to the current selection — the picked face in 3D, or the selected wall / sector floor in 2D. Slots render real texture thumbnails (with grey "empty" and red-cross "missing" placeholders), and the row refreshes whenever the project or texture set changes.

title: Unity package for Level Editor
excerpt: Welcome, and thanks for trying PapaiArt Level Editor. This project started as a love letter to the sector-based level design of the old shooters — fast iteration, hand-placed geometry, a grid you can feel under your feet. If that's the…
body:
Welcome, and thanks for trying PapaiArt Level Editor. This project started as a love letter to the sector-based level design of the old shooters — fast iteration, hand-placed geometry, a grid you can feel under your feet. If that's the kind of map-making you've been missing, you're in the right place. Build something weird, share what you make, and don't be shy about telling me what's broken — every map you draw makes the tool sharper.

Unity package: bundle export + auto-import

Polished the com.papaiart.leveleditor Unity package to make importing maps a one-drop operation.

Importer defaults cleaned up. Dropped textureScale from the inspector (it duplicated per-surface UV offsets already in the map JSON — now an internal constant TextureTileSize = 64). Set worldScale = 0.041675 as the default so the editor's grid lands at the right size in Unity meters. Flipped the flipWinding default to false — kept as a toggle for the rare case where faces look inverted.

File format rename. Map export now writes .pamap instead of .papaimap (shorter, cleaner). The ScriptedImporter, file-dialog filter, menu label, and package.json description all moved over together.

Bundle export from the C++ editor. File → Export for Unity (.pamap)… now writes three things side-by-side instead of just the map JSON:

  • <map>.pamap — the map itself
  • <map>.papaiproj — texture sidecar, mirrors the editor's project texture list but with paths relative to the bundle
  • Textures/ — copies of only the textures actually referenced by the map's floor/ceil/wall names (no project-wide dump)

New Unity-side .papaiproj ScriptedImporter. Picks up the sidecar and generates a MaterialDatabase sub-asset plus one Material sub-asset per texture name, wired to the matching PNG in Textures/. FLOOR_<n>, CEIL_<n>, WALL_<n> all point at the same material. Source-asset dependencies are registered so the database re-imports when a texture changes.

Sibling auto-discovery. When the .pamap importer's materialDatabase field is left empty, it scans the map's folder for a sibling .papaiproj and binds the generated database automatically. End-user workflow is now: export from the editor → drop the folder into Unity → drag the prefab into the scene. Zero clicks in between.

Docs. PDF user guides walking through the full flow with annotated screenshots.

Thank you. To everyone who tried the early builds, filed bug reports with screenshots, sketched maps that broke the importer in interesting ways, and kept asking "can it also do…" — this release exists because you didn't give up on it. Special thanks to the open-beta testers for their patience while sectors split themselves at the worst possible moments, and to the Blender, Doom, and Unity communities whose decades of accumulated wisdom on geometry, sloped sectors, and asset pipelines saved me from reinventing more than I already did. If your name belongs here and isn't, write to me — I'll fix it in the next release.

body:
The new version comes with a few but all the more useful features. One of them is support for multiple image formats, including PNG, JPG, and BMP.

The other addition is the ability to slide textures for a perfect fit. By pressing the TAB key to switch to 3D view, you can select the walls and use the arrow keys on your keyboard to position the textures.

Have fun!

If you notice any bugs or have any suggestions, I look forward to hearing them in the comments section.

En passant à la vue 3D à l'aide de la touche TAB, vous pouvez sélectionner les murs et positionner la texture à l'aide des flèches du clavier.

Amusez-vous bien !

Si vous remarquez des erreurs ou si vous avez des idées, je les attends dans la section des commentaires.
